title: The Position Machine
intro: Last session you found a shortcut. Today it gets a name and becomes a machine.

blocks.html:
At the dinner table you were set this: write the shortcut for 5, 8, 11, 14, … using n for the position.

Start + jumps × gap — and from the 1st term to the nth term is (n − 1) jumps. So:

term = 5 + (n − 1) × 3

One thing to be clear about before anything else. n is not a mystery number waiting to be solved. It is a slot. Feed the machine 7 and it hands you the 7th term. Feed it 100 and it hands you the 100th. Any position you like — that is the entire point of it.

blocks.hint: Careful with the jumps — there is one fewer jump than the position. For n = 4 that is 5 + 3 × 3.

parts.label: n = 4 (check it against the list)
parts._working: n = 4 → 5 + (4 − 1) × 3 = 5 + 9 = 14. Cross-check: the sequence is listed as 5, 8, 11, 14, so the 4th term is 14. The formula agrees with the list, which is why this part is here — it earns trust in the machine before the machine is asked to do anything clever.

parts.label: n = 100
parts._working: n = 100 → 5 + 99 × 3 = 5 + 297 = 302. (99 × 3: three hundreds less one 3.) Remember this number — it comes back in the reveal as a one-line check.

blocks.html:
5 + (n − 1) × 3 works, but it is clumsy. Multiply out the bracket:

(n − 1) × 3 = 3n − 3

So term = 5 + 3n − 3 = 3n + 2.

Test it before trusting it. n = 1 → 3 + 2 = 5 ✓. n = 4 → 12 + 2 = 14 ✓. n = 100 → 300 + 2 = 302 ✓ — the number you just worked out the long way, in one line.

Now look inside the rule, because this is the part worth keeping.

The 3 is the gap.
The +2 is where the sequence would have been at position zero — one step before it started.

This is called the nth term, and it is an entire sequence written in five characters.

blocks.prompt: The machine, in one line: n → × 3 → + 2 → term. Run it.
blocks.hint: Multiply the position by 3, then add 2. No counting.

parts.label: 7th term
parts._working: 3 × 7 + 2 = 23. Cross-check by counting on: 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23 — the 7th is 23 ✓.

parts.label: 40th term
parts._working: 3 × 40 + 2 = 120 + 2 = 122. Counting there would take all afternoon, which is the point.

blocks.html:
So far the rule has been handed to you. Now you make one, and it is only ever two moves.

Move 1 — the gap goes in front of n. A gap of 5 means the rule starts 5n.
Move 2 — step back one gap from the first term. That lands on the zeroth term, which is what you add on.

Watch it done on 7, 12, 17, 22, …

The gap is 5, so the rule starts 5n. Stepping back from 7 by 5 lands on 2. Rule: 5n + 2.

Then check on a term from the middle, never the first one: n = 3 → 15 + 2 = 17 ✓.

That is the whole method. Two moves and a check.

blocks.prompt: Your turn, one move at a time. The sequence is 4, 10, 16, 22, …
blocks.hint: Move 1 is the gap between neighbours. Move 2 steps back one gap from the 4.

parts.label: The gap
parts._working: 10 − 4 = 6, and 16 − 10 = 6, and 22 − 16 = 6 — constant, so this is a straight-line sequence and the method applies.

parts.label: The zeroth term (step back one gap from 4)
parts._working: 4 − 6 = −2. Unit 1's negatives earning their keep: the zeroth term is allowed to be below zero even though no term of the sequence is.

parts.label: So the rule is… (type it like 5n+2)
parts._working: Gap 6 in front of n, zeroth term −2 added on: 6n − 2. Middle check: n = 3 → 18 − 2 = 16 ✓, and n = 4 → 24 − 2 = 22 ✓. Accept covers the × and * forms (the engine maps both to x) and the reversed order, with hyphen-minus and unicode minus both listed because a tablet keyboard can produce either.

blocks.prompt: Boss rematch. The sequence that beat you on the diagnostic is back, and you have everything you need: 5, 8, 11, 14, …
blocks.hint: You watched this rule get tidied up earlier in the session. Then feed the position straight into it.

parts.label: The nth term rule
parts._working: Gap 8 − 5 = 3, zeroth term 5 − 3 = 2, so 3n + 2 — the rule derived in the reveal, now reproduced from the method rather than recalled. Middle check: n = 3 → 11 ✓.

parts.label: The 50th term
parts._working: 3 × 50 + 2 = 150 + 2 = 152. Three weeks ago this sequence got away from you over a single next-term; now its 50th term is one line.

blocks.prompt:
★ Optional, and a genuinely different trick — skip it with a clear conscience if you have had enough for today.

A machine you can run backwards is worth twice as much. Forwards is position → × 3 → + 2 → term. So backwards must be term → − 2 → ÷ 3 → position.

Worked for you first: is 62 in the sequence? 62 − 2 = 60, and 60 ÷ 3 = 20. Yes — 62 is the 20th term.

Now you try, the same two steps each time.
blocks.hint: Take off the 2, then divide by 3. If the division does not come out whole, the number simply is not in the sequence.

parts.label: 47 is which term?
parts._working: 47 − 2 = 45, and 45 ÷ 3 = 15, so 47 is the 15th term. Forward check: 3 × 15 + 2 = 47 ✓.

parts.label: Is 100 in the sequence? (yes/no)
parts._working: 100 − 2 = 98, and 98 ÷ 3 = 32.66… — not whole, so 100 cannot be a term. The terms either side are 3 × 32 + 2 = 98 and 3 × 33 + 2 = 101, so 100 falls in the gap. Answer: no. Note this is a PROOF, not a failed search — a better thing than checking, and the reason this ★ exists at all.

blocks.html:
🏔️ For the dinner table: two routes up the same crag. Height in metres after n pitches:

Route A: 3n + 2
Route B: 4n − 1

Route B starts lower and climbs faster, so somewhere the two must be level. Find the pitch where the climbers are at exactly the same height — and how high that is.

Then hand Dad the harder version: give him any two rules like these. Do the routes always meet? What has to be true about the two gaps for them never to? And can the meeting point land somewhere useless — like pitch 2½?

done.title: Machine built ✓
done.html:
The nth term: named, tidied, and then built from scratch by a method you can use on any straight-line sequence — gap in front of n, step back one gap, check in the middle.

The sequence that beat the diagnostic now gives up its 50th term in one line.

Next: Summit Puzzle: The Staircase — one problem, one session, and a pattern that breaks this machine completely. (It survives. You will need a different idea.)
